blocks.note: a side is a team, the word every match report uses
a real was a Spanish silver coin, so one of them is one from Spain

explanation.surface: A brilliant team with a Spaniard among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team' beside 'one from Spain' looks like a nod at Real Madrid, which is the picture the setter wants standing in front of the old coin the wordplay is really after.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellar → SIDEREAL: sidereal means measured by the stars, as a sidereal day is one turn of the Earth against them, so both are adjectives of the stars.

indicators.note: 'Possibly' admits the name given is only one instance of the kind wanted, not a synonym for it.
To bar a thing is to shut it out, so the letter named beside it is kept out of the word it came from.

blocks.note: the passage between rows of seats in a church or a plane is an aisle
the single letter A, the one thing barred from that word

explanation.surface: A man planted in a corridor and refusing to let anybody past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the island in the Irish Sea rather than a person, and the opening capital gives nothing away because every clue starts with one.
explanation.definitionFit: Man → ISLE: the Isle of Man is one island among many, so this is definition by example — 'possibly' is the setter saying so.

clue.text: Different types of KY jelly handed out

definitions.note: 'Different types' is plural where the answer names one man, but the phrase is a pair of names and the setter treats those two selves as the types themselves.

indicators.note: Letters put out are out of the order they arrived in, which is the sense being borrowed from the phrase around it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: Assorted lubricants being given away at some promotional stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handed out' looks like the whole instruction and only 'out' is: 'handed' is fodder, which is why the letters of 'KY jelly' on their own leave you six short.
explanation.definitionFit: Different types → JEKYLL AND HYDE: Stevenson's kindly doctor and his monstrous other self give the phrase for two utterly opposed characters in one person.

blocks.note: the adjective for an ally who does not waver, loyal through everything
the verb for stopping a flow, what a bandage does to bleeding

explanation.surface: A plant with a good sturdy stalk.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses land in different parts of speech, an adjective for the loyal friend and a verb for stopping blood, which is how two words make a whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm → STAUNCH: a staunch ally is unwavering, and to staunch a wound is to stem the flow — one spelling holding an adjective and a verb.

clue.text: One expression of approval or several

definitions.note: 'Several' is not a noun on its own: it leans back on the phrase in front of it, so the definition reads 'several expressions of approval', which is the plural the answer is.

blocks.note: A is the crossword's one, the article standing in for a single thing
the plainest word of agreement there is

explanation.surface: Somebody counting approval, one voice or a roomful of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition borrows the words in front of it: 'or several' means several of the approvals just described. In the Commons the ayes are the votes cast in favour of a motion.
explanation.definitionFit: several → AYES: the ayes are the votes in favour called in a parliamentary division, so several approvals is precisely what the plural names.

clue.text: Commotion when a bear seen near city

indicators.note: Things seen near one another are side by side, so these pieces are written one against the next with nothing between them.

blocks.note: Hull is the port city on the Humber in the north-east of England
the word is lifted from the surface exactly as it stands
Baloo is the bear who teaches Mowgli in The Jungle Book

explanation.surface: A city in uproar the moment a bear is spotted on the edge of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' wants a name rather than a species — Baloo, of The Jungle Book — and the city is a real one, Hull, sitting in the clue as though it were scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Commotion → HULLABALOO: the word is the noisy fuss a crowd makes, an uproar of voices rather than any disturbance in general.

clue.text: We’re disappointed when ostrich skin gets expensive

definitions.note: The definition is a statement where the answer is an exclamation: the clue gives what the phrase means rather than a phrase that could replace it in a sentence.

indicators.note: A skin is the covering on the outside, so what is kept here is only the letters at the two ends of the word.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of OSTRICH, the two the skin holds
dear means costly, still the everyday British word for a high price

explanation.surface: The price of ostrich leather climbing, and somebody's face falling at the news.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a report on the leather trade, and 'gets expensive' is not describing any skin at all — it hands over an ordinary word for costly.
explanation.definitionFit: We’re disappointed → OH DEAR: the exclamation is the mild noise of dismay English makes at bad news, so it says what the definition states flatly.

clue.text: Long for captive juvenile’s frivolous past

blocks.note: to miss somebody is to long for them
pent means shut in, as a captive is
a juvenile is a young person not yet grown, a five-letter word for an adolescent

explanation.surface: Yearning for the wild early years of a young prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long for' sits at the front where a definition usually goes and it is wordplay. 'Pent' survives now mostly inside 'pent-up', but on its own it means shut in.
explanation.definitionFit: frivolous past → MISSPENT YOUTH: the set phrase is the standard one for early years thrown away on fun, and no single word of it carries the sense alone.

blocks.note: in the sense of no more than that, as in 'just a scratch'
a lake or pond, the old word for standing water that survives in English place names

explanation.surface: A drink turning out to be nothing but water.
explanation.walkthrough: The belittling adjective and a northern word for a lake share a spelling and nothing else, which is how two words manage to be an entire clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Just → MERE: mere means nothing more than, as in a mere child; and a mere is a lake, water lying still in the old sense.

clue.text: Solvers being solvers with every other beauty product

indicators.note: A product is what comes out once things have been worked together, so the letters arrive combined into something new instead of in their own order.
'Every other' means every second one, so only alternate letters of the word beside it are picked up.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters — the clue's second use of the word
the second, fourth and sixth letters of bEaUtY

explanation.surface: Crossword solvers behaving exactly as solvers do, with cosmetics from the counter thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does both jobs: 'Solvers' is the definition, and its second appearance is the fodder. 'Beauty product' splits too, so only the first of those two words hands over letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Solvers → YOURSELVES: the puzzle is talking to the people solving it, so the plural pronoun stands in for the very readers the clue is naming.

clue.text: Officer sounding a bit of a nut

indicators.note: 'Sounding' asks for the noise a word makes rather than its spelling, which is the only place these two words meet.

blocks.note: an army officer is a colonel, and British speech puts an R in the middle of that word and no L at all

explanation.surface: An officer who strikes everyone as slightly mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a nut' looks like an instruction to take a few letters out of 'a nut', and it is the definition read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: a bit of a nut → KERNEL: the kernel is the soft part inside the shell, which is exactly the bit of a nut anybody eats.

blocks.note: a hanky that might be silk is not the paper kind, and the wordplay opens with that denial
the paper sort of handkerchief is a tissue

explanation.surface: Somebody ruling that whether the handkerchief happens to be silk makes no difference.
explanation.walkthrough: Say what a silk hanky is not, then move the gaps between the words along one letter, and a phrase for something beside the point comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: irrelevant → NOT AT ISSUE: a matter not at issue is one the argument does not turn on, so it has no bearing — both sit as adjectives after 'is'.

clue.text: Last users promoting the ultimate in rock’n’roll hits

indicators.note: To promote a thing is to move it up the order, so the letter picked out travels nearer the front of the word holding it.

blocks.note: a last is the foot-shaped block a shoemaker builds a shoe on, so the people who use lasts are cobblers
its final letter, the L, is the one singled out to move; the word hands over nothing of its own

explanation.surface: The last few listeners still pushing the greatest rock and roll records up the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: A last is the shoemaker's foot-shaped block, so its users are cobblers, and only one letter of that word travels: the L that the end of rock’n’roll points at.
explanation.definitionFit: hits → CLOBBERS: to clobber somebody is to hit them a heavy blow, and both words are given here in the same third-person form.

blocks.note: the grape's name breaks into three scraps, P / in / ot, and this is the last of them
the first of those scraps, one letter standing alone

explanation.surface: A wine list, and somebody plumping for the Pinot.
explanation.walkthrough: The wine is not a synonym for anything here: its name reads as an instruction, P in OT. Setters call this a reverse clue, and the question mark is the warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Choose → OPT: to opt is to pick between the things on offer, the verb that takes 'for' and means settling on one of them.

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so those two openings change places.

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat, said "kat"; it gives away its opening K and takes the FL coming back the other way
the door a cat lets itself in by is a flap; it hands over its FL and collects the K that has just been let go

explanation.surface: A man called Tom submitting an entry to Spooner's hat competition.
explanation.walkthrough: A tom is a male cat and its entry is the flap in the door — say those two words, trade the noises at their fronts, and a hat comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: headgear → FLAT CAP: the cloth cap with a small stiff peak, the working man's hat of northern England, is one particular piece of headgear.

blocks.note: the head of SKIN is its first letter, so only the S survives the operation
the speaker at a meeting is the one doing the talking

explanation.surface: A shaven-headed orator with somebody unwelcome loitering at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinhead' is one word doing two jobs, the word SKIN and the instruction to keep only its head, while the surface's shaven orator is there to be looked at instead.
explanation.definitionFit: undesirable presence → STALKER: a stalker is the person nobody wants near them, defined here by the effect of being followed rather than by the following.

clue.text: Cast a spell on the way in

blocks.note: the verb for holding somebody spellbound, stressed on its second syllable
the door or gateway you come in by, stressed on its first syllable

explanation.surface: A magician bewitching the guests as they come through the door.
explanation.walkthrough: One set of letters said two ways — EN-trance the doorway, en-TRANCE the enchantment — which is why the clue can lay the two meanings side by side with no joint between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast a spell on → ENTRANCE: the verb means to delight as though by magic, and the noun, said with the stress moved, is the door you come in by.

clue.text: Juliet exits crossing to get ointment

indicators.note: Whatever exits leaves the place it was in, so the letter named goes out of the word around it.

blocks.note: a crossing of roads is a junction
Juliet is J in the radio alphabet, and it is the letter that walks out

explanation.surface: Juliet stepping off the crossroads to fetch some ointment.
explanation.walkthrough: Juliet is the J of the radio alphabet, Alpha to Zulu, and 'crossing' is a meeting of roads rather than anything to do with a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: ointment → UNCTION: unction is the oil used in anointing, as in the last rites' extreme unction, so it names the salve itself.

clue.text: Big beast that was unsettling to nomads

indicators.note: Something unsettling refuses to settle, and letters that will not settle do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Wandering herders unnerved by something enormous out on the plain.
explanation.walkthrough: Nomads and a big beast belong in the same sentence, which is what hides the letters: the fodder is the very people the beast is upsetting.
explanation.definitionFit: Big beast → MASTODON: the mastodon was the elephant-sized browser of the Ice Age, so the plain phrase names the animal by its size and kind.

blocks.note: the commercial between programmes is an ad, short for advertisement
a rift is a split, whether in a rock face or in a party

explanation.surface: A company's sales department wandering away from the plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial division' reads as one department of a firm, and the wordplay wants the two words apart, the first of them in its television sense.
explanation.definitionFit: off course → ADRIFT: a boat adrift has no steerage and goes wherever the current takes it, which is precisely not where it was headed.

blocks.note: Bravo is B in the radio alphabet, the one spelt out over the airwaves
lotto is the numbers game people gamble on

explanation.surface: A shout of approval for a gambler who is thoroughly drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Bravo is B in the radio alphabet, worth owning along with its twenty-five companions, and the comma after it turns the rest of the clue into a cheer.
explanation.definitionFit: drunk → BLOTTO: blotto is the slang adjective for being completely drunk, well past merry, and it has no other sense to confuse it with.

indicators.note: 'In' puts the word before it inside the word after it rather than alongside, so one splits to let the other sit at its centre.

blocks.note: a bit is a part of something, a piece broken off
to dine is to eat, the plain word for it

explanation.surface: Told to eat a little of the meal and then go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dine in' reads as one phrase about eating at home, and the wordplay takes the words apart, with the middle one saying where the first of them goes.
explanation.definitionFit: leave → BEAT IT: the slang imperative means clear off, and both are verbs for going away, though only one of them is something you shout.

clue.text: Toast giving thanks to Schubert composition

indicators.note: A composition is something put together out of parts, so the letters beside it are being set in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: ta is the everyday British way of saying thanks
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A dinner toast raised in thanks to Schubert and one of his pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toast' is the food rather than the speech the surface promises, and TA supplies the two letters the composer's name is short of.
explanation.definitionFit: Toast → BRUSCHETTA: the Italian starter is grilled bread rubbed with garlic and oil, so it is toast served as a dish in its own right.

clue.text: They care when warm clothing not provided and we fully support that

definitions.note: The definition is a sentence where the answer is a shout: the clue gives what a meeting means when it calls this out, not a phrase that could replace it grammatically.

indicators.note: Clothing is what covers a thing on the outside, so a word given none of it loses the letters at each of its two ends.

blocks.note: THEY undressed of its outer T and Y
CARE with the C and E at its ends taken off
WHEN stripped of its opening W and closing N
WARM without the W and M that cover it

explanation.surface: People who mind that others are left without warm clothes, and a voice backing them completely.
explanation.walkthrough: Four four-letter words in a row, each with two letters buried at its centre; the sentence reads as a plea about the cold and hands over the same shout twice, once across and once down.
explanation.definitionFit: we fully support that → HEAR HEAR: the cry is what a chamber calls when it agrees with a speaker, so the shout means exactly the sentence given.

indicators.note: 'In' places the letter before it inside the word that follows, not beside it.

blocks.note: a fund is a pot of money set aside
love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

explanation.surface: Romance turning up where the money is.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is the tennis nought, no score at all, and the little story about finding romance in wealth is what keeps a single letter out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Discovered → FOUND: found is the past tense of find, so it matches the definition's tense as well as its sense of coming across something.

clue.text: Crude oil charge mostly makes wealthy and powerful individual

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the last letter, so the final one is left behind.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, the three letters of the word itself
CHARGE with its final letter dropped

explanation.surface: The price of crude oil making somebody enormously rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crude' does two jobs at once, describing the oil in the surface and ordering the shuffle in the wordplay, so nothing in the sentence looks like an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: wealthy and powerful individual → OLIGARCH: an oligarch is one of the few who hold power, and in current usage a very rich businessman with political weight.
